papers.title: Insights into the role of oxidative stress in the pathology of Friedreich ataxia using peroxidation resistant polyunsaturated fatty acids.
papers.summary: Deuterated linoleic acid and α-linolenic acid rescued oxidative-stress-challenged yeast, murine, and primary human Friedreich ataxia cell models while reducing lipid peroxidation; non-deuterated forms were toxic under the same challenge. The protective effects of deuterated PUFAs and idebenone were additive in the murine model, supporting lipid isotope stabilization as a potential therapeutic strategy, but efficacy in patients and the intracellular site of action remain unestablished.
papers.why: The paper experimentally shows that peroxidation-resistant deuterated PUFAs rescue oxidatively stressed FRDA cells, reduce lipid peroxidation, and have an additive effect with idebenone.

papers.title: Safety and Efficacy of Omaveloxolone in Friedreich Ataxia (MOXIe Study).
papers.summary: In the 48-week MOXIe phase 2 trial, omaveloxolone significantly improved neurological function in patients with Friedreich ataxia relative to placebo, primarily reflected by improvement in the modified Friedreich's Ataxia Rating Scale. Omaveloxolone also improved several biochemical measures, but hierarchical secondary efficacy endpoints were not statistically significant, and treatment was associated with early adverse events and transient, reversible aminotransferase elevations without demonstrated liver injury.
papers.why: The randomized phase 2 MOXIe trial reports that omaveloxolone significantly improved neurological function versus placebo in patients with Friedreich ataxia.

papers.title: Surgery for equinovarus deformity in Friedreich's ataxia improves mobility and independence.
papers.summary: In a Level IV case series of 36 patients with Friedreich's ataxia, surgery for fixed equinovarus deformity was followed by improved function and mobility, although three of seven surgically treated patients experienced significant complications. The study also used splinting, botulinum toxin Type A, rehabilitation, the Barthel index, and the Functional Independence Measure as components of management or outcome assessment.
papers.why: This therapeutic study shows that management of equinovarus deformity can improve mobility and independence in Friedreich ataxia.

papers.title: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of interferon-γ 1b in Friedreich Ataxia.
papers.summary: A 26-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial found no benefit of interferon-γ 1b on neurological outcomes and no increase in whole-blood or buccal-cell frataxin in 92 children and young adults with Friedreich ataxia. The study was limited by high mFARS variability and insufficient power for small effects or short treatment periods, while uncontrolled open-label observations suggested possible modest stabilization that requires confirmation.
papers.why: This randomized controlled trial directly tested interferon-gamma-1b in FRDA using mFARS and related clinical outcomes, finding no clear treatment benefit after six months.

papers.title: PGC-1alpha down-regulation affects the antioxidant response in Friedreich's ataxia.
papers.summary: FRDA patient fibroblasts and KIKO mouse tissues show reduced PGC-1α and SOD2 expression and a blunted SOD2 response to oxidative stress. Pharmacological activation of PPARγ with pioglitazone or AMPK with AICAR restores SOD2 induction in FRDA cells, while pioglitazone increases PGC-1α and SOD2 in the cerebellum and spinal cord of KIKO mice without increasing frataxin.
papers.why: Pioglitazone and AICAR restored the deficient antioxidant response in Friedreich ataxia cells, while pioglitazone increased SOD2 in relevant tissues of a disease mouse model.

papers.title: Effect of Itraconazole, a CYP3A4 Inhibitor, and Rifampin, a CYP3A4 Inducer, on the Pharmacokinetics of Vatiquinone.
papers.summary: In this phase 1, open-label drug–drug interaction study in healthy adults, itraconazole increased vatiquinone exposure approximately 3.5-fold for Cmax and 2.9-fold for AUC0-inf, whereas rifampin reduced exposure to 0.64-fold and 0.54-fold, respectively. These findings confirm that CYP3A4 contributes importantly to vatiquinone metabolism, while the clinical relevance of exposure changes during concomitant use of CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers remains to be determined.
papers.why: The randomized pharmacokinetic study quantifies how CYP3A4 inhibition and induction alter vatiquinone exposure, providing actionable interaction data for Friedreich ataxia drug development.

papers.title: Treatment for speech disorder in Friedreich ataxia and other hereditary ataxia syndromes.
papers.summary: This systematic review found insufficient low- or very-low-quality evidence to determine whether any tested treatment improves speech disorder in Friedreich ataxia or other hereditary ataxias. Betamethasone and riluzole produced statistically significant speech improvements in selected mixed ataxia populations, while alpha-tocopheryl quinone improved an overall disease rating but not its speech subscale in Friedreich ataxia, and most other pharmaceutical treatments and rehabilitation effects were null or not sustained.
papers.why: This systematic review evaluates 14 clinical trials involving 721 patients and reports tested pharmaceutical treatments and speech outcome assessments in Friedreich ataxia and related hereditary ataxias.

papers.title: Safety and efficacy of (+)-epicatechin in subjects with Friedreich's ataxia: A phase II, open-label, prospective study.
papers.summary: In a 24-week phase II open-label study, oral (+)-epicatechin was generally well tolerated and was associated with improvements in selected cardiac structure and function measures in a subset of participants with Friedreich's ataxia. The primary neurological outcomes did not show statistically significant improvement, although FARS/mFARS scores improved in 5 of 9 evaluable participants and the 8-m walk and 9-peg hole test improved in some participants.
papers.why: A phase II Friedreich ataxia study reports safety, neurological and cardiac outcomes for (+)-epicatechin and measures of treatment response.

papers.title: Triple therapy with darbepoetin alfa, idebenone, and riboflavin in Friedreich's ataxia: an open-label trial.
papers.summary: The paper reports an open-label clinical pilot study of triple therapy with darbepoetin alfa, idebenone, and riboflavin in nine female patients with Friedreich's ataxia. Treatment was tolerated, and the authors observed statistically nonsignificant improvement in ataxia, a small reduction in disease progression during the first two years, and statistically nonsignificant improvement in left ventricular mass index with stable echocardiographic parameters.
papers.why: An open-label FRDA trial directly tested triple darbepoetin alfa, idebenone, and riboflavin therapy and measured ataxia and cardiac outcomes.

papers.title: Regional siderosis: a new challenge for iron chelation therapy.
papers.summary: This review proposes that Friedreich ataxia is a regional siderosis disorder in which abnormal iron distribution creates toxic labile iron alongside impaired essential iron-dependent functions. It reports that oral deferiprone, often initially combined with idebenone, reduced cardiac hypertrophy and cerebellar dentate-nucleus R2* values in adolescent patients but did not alter plasma iron parameters or complete blood counts, while large confirmatory trials remain necessary.
papers.why: The paper develops and tests a dual-action iron-redistribution strategy using deferiprone in cellular, translational, and clinical settings relevant to Friedreich ataxia.

papers.title: Long-term effect of epoetin alfa on clinical and biochemical markers in friedreich ataxia.
papers.summary: In a 48-week double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, epoetin alfa did not improve peak oxygen uptake or most secondary endpoints in 56 patients with Friedreich ataxia. Upper-limb performance measured by the 9-hole peg test improved, but the authors considered a symptomatic benefit possible rather than established.
papers.why: This Friedreich ataxia trial directly tests epoetin alfa and reports efficacy, biochemical, cardiac, neurological, safety, and quality-of-life outcomes.

papers.title: HDAC inhibitors correct frataxin deficiency in a Friedreich ataxia mouse model.
papers.summary: The HDAC inhibitor compound 106 increased FXN transcription and restored frataxin protein to near wild-type levels in the central nervous system and heart of KIKI mice carrying a (GAA)230 repeat, with no apparent acute toxicity. Treatment also shifted most frataxin-deficiency-associated transcriptional changes toward wild-type levels, while patient-derived lymphocytes showed increased FXN mRNA and histone acetylation in vitro.
papers.why: Compound 106 restored frataxin expression in patient cells and normalized frataxin levels and disease-associated gene-expression changes in a Friedreich ataxia mouse model without reported acute toxicity.

papers.title: Safety, pharmacodynamics, and potential benefit of omaveloxolone in Friedreich ataxia.
papers.summary: In a 12-week Phase 2 randomized, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, omaveloxolone was generally well tolerated and produced dose-dependent pharmacodynamic changes, with neurological improvement measured by mFARS maximal at 160 mg/day. The primary exercise endpoint did not improve, and other performance and quality-of-life endpoints were generally null, although patients without pes cavus showed greater mFARS and exercise responses.
papers.why: A randomized phase II study provides patient data on dose-dependent omaveloxolone effects, pharmacodynamic biomarkers, and mFARS outcomes in Friedreich ataxia.

papers.title: Novel Nrf2-Inducer Prevents Mitochondrial Defects and Oxidative Stress in Friedreich's Ataxia Models.
papers.summary: The paper shows that omaveloxolone activates the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway and ameliorates Complex I inhibition, oxidative stress, mitochondrial depolarization, and cell death in cerebellar granule neurons from two Friedreich ataxia mouse models and in primary fibroblasts from patients with Friedreich ataxia. The study found no significant difference in basal mitochondrial membrane potential between patient and control fibroblasts.
papers.why: The study tests an NRF2 inducer in two Friedreich ataxia mouse models and patient fibroblasts, demonstrating restoration of Complex I activity and protection from oxidative stress.

papers.title: Progression of Friedreich ataxia: quantitative characterization over 5 years.
papers.summary: In an 812-person, 5-year natural-history cohort, the study found that Friedreich ataxia progression is most rapid in younger patients and is strongly associated with baseline severity and, after adjustment, guanine-adenine-adenine repeat length. It also shows that FARS, Modified FARS, and performance composites become more reproducible over longer follow-up and that younger enrollment can substantially reduce clinical-trial sample-size requirements.
papers.why: Provides long-term quantitative natural-history data and validated clinical outcome measures for tracking Friedreich ataxia progression and planning clinical trials.

papers.title: Functional genomic analysis of frataxin deficiency reveals tissue-specific alterations and identifies the PPARgamma pathway as a therapeutic target in Friedreich's ataxia.
papers.summary: The paper identifies tissue-specific transcriptional effects of frataxin deficiency and implicates dysregulation of the PPARγ/PGC1A/SREBP1 pathway in lipogenesis, altered muscle fiber composition, cardiomyopathy, and insulin resistance. Human cells and non-diabetic patients showed reduced PGC1A and insulin sensitivity, while PGC1A knockdown reduced frataxin in fibroblasts, suggesting a positive-feedback mechanism and a potential therapeutic target.
papers.why: The study identifies PPARgamma as a therapeutically targetable pathway and shows that genetic modulation of it changes frataxin levels in FRDA-relevant models and patient cells.

papers.title: Prolonged treatment with pimelic o-aminobenzamide HDAC inhibitors ameliorates the disease phenotype of a Friedreich ataxia mouse model.
papers.summary: Prolonged subcutaneous treatment with pimelic o-aminobenzamide HDAC inhibitors 106, 109, and 136 ameliorated selected disease manifestations in the YG8R Friedreich ataxia mouse model, with 109 producing the strongest molecular, biochemical, histological, and behavioral effects. Increased FXN-locus histone acetylation and brain frataxin protein were not accompanied by a significant increase in brain FXN mRNA, and the model's neurological phenotype remained mild.
papers.why: Long-term treatment with three HDAC inhibitors improved selected disease phenotypes, frataxin expression, brain aconitase activity, and neuronal pathology in an FRDA mouse model.

papers.title: Inducible and reversible phenotypes in a novel mouse model of Friedreich's Ataxia.
papers.summary: The study establishes the inducible FRDAkd mouse as a reversible, multisystem model of adult frataxin deficiency that reproduces major motor, cardiac, neurological, mitochondrial, pathological, and transcriptomic features of Friedreich ataxia. Withdrawal of doxycycline restored near-normal FXN expression and substantially reversed functional, cardiac, retinal, molecular, and some dorsal-root-ganglion abnormalities, while spinal-cord abnormalities recovered only mildly, demonstrating that substantial disease manifestations reflect reversible cellular dysfunction.
papers.why: The study develops an inducible mouse model that reproduces multiple Friedreich ataxia phenotypes and tests the reversibility of pathology after restoring frataxin.

papers.title: Frataxin levels in peripheral tissue in Friedreich ataxia.
papers.summary: Peripheral frataxin levels measured in buccal cells and blood reflect Friedreich ataxia severity, GAA repeat length, age, and the specific FXN mutation, although point mutations can produce major tissue-specific discrepancies. Mutation-dependent experiments showed reduced frataxin expression or mitochondrial localization for G130V and I154F, preserved mitochondrial localization and immunoreactive levels for R165C, and red-blood-cell retention of frataxin with early start-codon mutations.
papers.why: The study validates peripheral frataxin measurement in blood and buccal cells as a disease-related biomarker and links it to neurological ratings and specific FXN mutations.

papers.title: Long intronic GAA*TTC repeats induce epigenetic changes and reporter gene silencing in a molecular model of Friedreich ataxia.
papers.summary: The paper develops and validates GFP_(GAA•TTC)560 HEK293 reporter cell lines that reproduce the repeat-associated transcriptional silencing, reduced reporter expression, and chromatin changes of expanded FXN alleles in Friedreich ataxia. The model responds similarly to selected histone deacetylase inhibitors and is proposed for high-throughput screening of compounds that relieve GAA•TTC-mediated repression.
papers.why: The study developed a molecular FRDA model that reproduces epigenetic silencing and showed that HDAC inhibitors can restore reporter expression, enabling high-throughput therapeutic screens.

papers.title: Targeting NRF2 for the Treatment of Friedreich's Ataxia: A Comparison among Drugs.
papers.summary: In patient-derived FRDA fibroblasts, six redox-active compounds all increased NRF2 expression but produced distinct downstream molecular profiles; sulforaphane, dimethyl fumarate, N-acetylcysteine, and EPI-743 also significantly increased FXN expression. The findings identify NRF2 modulation and the Keap-1/DJ-1/p62 axis as candidate therapeutic or drug-screening mechanisms, although the experiments were conducted in fibroblasts rather than affected nervous-system tissue.
papers.why: Six candidate drugs were compared directly in Friedreich ataxia patient fibroblasts, identifying distinct NRF2 downstream effects and potential combination strategies.

papers.title: Loss of Frataxin induces iron toxicity, sphingolipid synthesis, and Pdk1/Mef2 activation, leading to neurodegeneration.
papers.summary: The paper identifies an iron toxicity–sphingolipid synthesis–Pdk1/Mef2 pathway downstream of frataxin loss in a Drosophila fh mutant model, with reduced iron, inhibited sphingolipid synthesis, or reduced Pdk1/Mef2 suppressing neurodegeneration. Human FXN rescues the fly phenotype, and dihydrosphingosine activates Mef2 through PDK1 in Neuro-2A cells, but whether the pathway operates in human Friedreich ataxia remains untested.
papers.why: The study directly models FXN-loss neurodegeneration in flies and tests interventions that suppress neurodegeneration through the iron-sphingolipid-Pdk1-Mef2 pathway.

papers.title: High Levels of Frataxin Overexpression Lead to Mitochondrial and Cardiac Toxicity in Mouse Models.
papers.summary: AAV-mediated FXN gene replacement improved or rescued cardiac disease in Mck mice when expression was controlled, but cardiac FXN expression above approximately 20-fold normal caused mitochondrial, cardiomyocyte, and heart toxicity, whereas expression up to 9-fold was uneventful. Toxicity was tissue-specific: liver tolerated expression up to approximately 90- to 97-fold without detectable acute cellular or mitochondrial toxicity.
papers.why: Mouse experiments establish tolerable cardiac FXN overexpression up to ninefold and identify mitochondrial and cardiac toxicity above twentyfold, providing dosing and safety guidance for gene therapy.

papers.title: Nrf2-Inducers Counteract Neurodegeneration in Frataxin-Silenced Motor Neurons: Disclosing New Therapeutic Targets for Friedreich's Ataxia.
papers.summary: In frataxin-silenced mouse motor neurons, sulforaphane and dimethyl fumarate increased Nrf2/Nrf2-ARE signaling, antioxidant enzyme expression, and glutathione homeostasis while promoting axonal regrowth. Sulforaphane also increased NRF2 and downstream antioxidant transcripts in fibroblasts from three patients with Friedreich ataxia, while reduced NRF2 expression in patient PBMCs supported its exploration as a blood redox biomarker.
papers.why: Sulforaphane induced antioxidant enzymes and improved neurite number and extension in frataxin-deficient motor-neuron and patient fibroblast cultures.

papers.title: A combined nucleic acid and protein analysis in Friedreich ataxia: implications for diagnosis, pathogenesis and clinical trial design.
papers.summary: The study shows that peripheral-blood FXN mRNA and frataxin protein levels are reduced in Friedreich ataxia and can distinguish classic Friedreich ataxia or point-mutation disease from healthy controls. However, substantial overlap among late-onset patients, carriers, and controls limits prediction of late-onset disease, and PBMC measurements may not reflect levels in affected cells.
papers.why: This study demonstrates a combined nucleic-acid and protein testing strategy that identifies classic and point-mutation FRDA and quantifies residual frataxin for diagnosis and trial design.

papers.title: Autophagy induction extends lifespan and reduces lipid content in response to frataxin silencing in C. elegans.
papers.summary: Partial frataxin suppression in Caenorhabditis elegans induces an intact, cep-1-regulated autophagic flux that reduces lipid storage and extends lifespan; bec-1 is required for these effects. FRDA-derived human lymphoblasts also show increased autophagy with reduced frataxin expression, supporting autophagy as a conserved compensatory response and a candidate therapeutic intervention for Friedreich ataxia.
papers.why: The study experimentally establishes a frataxin-deficient worm model and shows that autophagy induction is a testable therapeutic strategy with supporting evidence in human FRDA cells.

papers.title: Deferiprone targets aconitase: implication for Friedreich's ataxia treatment.
papers.summary: The paper reports that deferiprone, a mitochondrial iron chelator, causes dose- and time-dependent loss of aconitase activity in control and Friedreich ataxia fibroblasts and in frataxin-depleted SK-N-AS cells. Aconitase impairment preceded or accompanied major decreases in cell proliferation, supporting the risk of excessive mitochondrial iron depletion during iron-chelation approaches for Friedreich ataxia.
papers.why: The study directly tests deferiprone-related iron chelation in Friedreich ataxia cellular systems and identifies aconitase activity as an exposure-related pharmacodynamic safety measure.

papers.title: Pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the novel Nrf2 activator omaveloxolone in primates.
papers.summary: Oral omaveloxolone produced dose-proportional systemic exposure and tissue distribution in cynomolgus monkeys, with dose-dependent induction of Nrf2 target genes in liver, lung, brain, and PBMCs. Clinical PK data and initial Phase II results in Friedreich’s ataxia indicate that doses of at least 80 mg achieved exposures consistent with monkey Nrf2 activation and were associated with neurological-function and serum-biomarker improvements.
papers.why: Primate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data establish tissue exposure and NRF2 biomarkers that directly support omaveloxolone dosing in Friedreich ataxia.

papers.title: Predictors of loss of ambulation in Friedreich's ataxia.
papers.summary: In the FA-COMS natural history cohort, loss of ambulation in Friedreich ataxia was preceded by an ordered loss of upright-stability functions, particularly in patients with onset before age 15. The paper proposes that these functional milestones and loss of ambulation can stratify patients, estimate individual progression, support sample-size planning, and serve as clinically meaningful outcomes in clinical trials.
papers.why: The study derives and validates outcome measures and a stratification model for loss of ambulation using longitudinal FA-COMS data.

papers.title: In vivo overexpression of frataxin causes toxicity mediated by iron-sulfur cluster deficiency.
papers.summary: AAV9-CAG-FXN produced high frataxin expression and only partial, transient improvement of cardiac dysfunction in MCK-Fxn mice, while supraphysiological expression caused liver injury, Fe-S cluster deficiency, weight loss, and premature death. The N146K frataxin variant largely prevented these toxic effects, showing that toxicity requires frataxin binding to the mitochondrial Fe-S cluster core complex.
papers.why: The study tests AAV9-mediated frataxin delivery in mice and identifies dose-dependent overexpression toxicity and iron-sulfur-cluster deficiency relevant to FRDA gene-therapy development.

papers.title: Future Prospects of Gene Therapy for Friedreich's Ataxia.
papers.summary: This review concludes that viral-vector delivery of FXN or brain-derived neurotrophic factor is a promising preclinical approach for Friedreich ataxia, with AAV9 and AAVrh10 offering favorable central nervous system delivery. The main barriers are delivery across affected tissues, immunotoxicity, and transgene overexpression toxicity, while the YG8JR mouse is presented as the most genetically faithful model for evaluating therapies.
papers.why: The review reports promising viral-vector FXN or neurotrophin treatments tested in Friedreich ataxia mouse models and discusses actionable delivery and safety considerations.

papers.title: The first cellular models based on frataxin missense mutations that reproduce spontaneously the defects associated with Friedreich ataxia.
papers.summary: The study generated stable humanized murine fibroblast models carrying FRDA-associated frataxin variants G130V or I154F that spontaneously reproduce multiple biochemical features of Friedreich ataxia while remaining viable. I154F produced the more severe phenotype, including mitochondrial iron accumulation, broader iron-sulfur cluster enzyme deficits, and increased susceptibility to oxidative stress, supporting the models' use for mechanistic studies and pharmacological screening.
papers.why: Develops cellular models that reproduce multiple FRDA biochemical phenotypes and are explicitly positioned for large-scale drug screening.

papers.title: Propensity matched comparison of omaveloxolone treatment to Friedreich ataxia natural history data.
papers.summary: In a post hoc propensity-matched comparison of 136 omaveloxolone-treated MOXIe extension patients with 136 untreated FACOMS natural-history controls, omaveloxolone slowed 3-year Friedreich ataxia progression as measured by mFARS by 55% (3.0 versus 6.6 points; difference −3.6; nominal p=0.0001). Results favored omaveloxolone in all primary and sensitivity analysis populations, while the authors noted limitations from the nonrandomized external-control design, unmatched prognostic variables, differing assessment schedules, and lack of a placebo-effect estimate.
papers.why: The study directly compares three years of omaveloxolone treatment with a propensity-matched natural-history cohort and shows slower mFARS progression, while demonstrating a reusable trial-analysis method.

papers.title: Interactions of iron-bound frataxin with ISCU and ferredoxin on the cysteine desulfurase complex leading to Fe-S cluster assembly.
papers.summary: The study shows that human frataxin binds one Fe2+ and associates with the NFS1–ISD11–acyl carrier protein machinery, with ISCU strengthening that interaction. Under anaerobic in vitro conditions, L-cysteine and a reductant are jointly required to trigger Fe2+ release, and Fe2+-FXN can serve as the sole iron donor for ferredoxin-supported Fe-S cluster assembly.
papers.why: The paper directly tests frataxin interactions and iron transfer in the human mitochondrial Fe-S cluster assembly machinery using concrete biophysical assays.

papers.title: Plasma Markers of Neurodegeneration Are Raised in Friedreich's Ataxia.
papers.summary: In a cohort of 33 people with Friedreich ataxia and 13 age-matched controls, plasma neurofilament-light chain, glial fibrillary acidic protein, and ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 concentrations were significantly elevated, whereas total tau was not significantly different. The Simoa Neurology 4-Plex assay produced strongly concordant NfL results to an established singleplex assay, but none of the four biomarkers was independently associated with GAA repeat length or clinical severity after relevant adjustment.
papers.why: Provides patient data validating NfL, GFAP, and UCHL1 as accessible plasma neurodegeneration biomarkers and demonstrating a multiplex assay for monitoring Friedreich ataxia.

papers.title: E3 Ligase RNF126 Directly Ubiquitinates Frataxin, Promoting Its Degradation: Identification of a Potential Therapeutic Target for Friedreich Ataxia.
papers.summary: The study identifies RNF126 as the E3 ubiquitin ligase that binds and directly ubiquitinates frataxin precursor, promoting its proteasomal degradation and thereby limiting production of mature frataxin. RNF126 knockdown increased precursor and mature frataxin in engineered HEK293 cells and restored accumulation of mature frataxin in fibroblasts from two patients with Friedreich ataxia, supporting RNF126 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy that remains experimentally unvalidated in patients.
papers.why: Identifies RNF126 as an E3 ligase that degrades frataxin and shows that its depletion restores frataxin accumulation in patient-derived cells.

papers.title: Nrf2 Induction Re-establishes a Proper Neuronal Differentiation Program in Friedreich's Ataxia Neural Stem Cells.
papers.summary: The study shows that frataxin-deficient KIKO mouse neural stem cells have reduced proliferation and clonogenicity, premature neuronal differentiation, reduced neuronal complexity, oxidative stress, impaired Complex I activity, and deficient Nrf2/ARE signaling during embryonic neurogenesis. The Nrf2 inducers sulforaphane (SFN) and EPI-743 restored antioxidant signaling and partially improved redox status, proliferation, clonogenicity, differentiation, and neuronal morphology, although the effects on proliferation and clonogenicity were not statistically significant and rescue was incomplete.
papers.why: Shows that enhancing Nrf2 activity corrects proliferation, stemness, and differentiation defects in neural stem cells from a Frataxin-deficient Friedreich ataxia model.

papers.title: Characterization of a new N-terminally acetylated extra-mitochondrial isoform of frataxin in human erythrocytes.
papers.summary: The study identifies N-terminally acetylated frataxin isoform E (76–210) as the predominant frataxin form in human erythrocytes and shows that overexpressed isoform E can be proteolytically converted into extra-mitochondrial mature frataxin in HEK 293 cells. Isoform-specific LC-MS can separately quantify erythrocytic isoform E and mature mitochondrial frataxin, potentially simplifying whole-blood biomarker analysis for Friedreich ataxia natural-history studies and treatment monitoring, although this application was not validated in Friedreich ataxia patients in the present study.
papers.why: The study identified and quantified an extra-mitochondrial erythrocyte frataxin isoform and proposed isoform-specific blood measurement for Friedreich ataxia monitoring.

papers.title: The NRF2 Signaling Network Defines Clinical Biomarkers and Therapeutic Opportunity in Friedreich's Ataxia.
papers.summary: This review identifies defective NRF2 signaling as a mechanistic and potentially actionable component of Friedreich’s ataxia, in which frataxin deficiency causes mitochondrial iron accumulation, impaired iron–sulfur cluster biosynthesis, and increased oxidative stress. It surveys NRF2-directed interventions and proposes NRF2-regulated molecular markers, including NCF2, PDLIM1, NQO1, glutathione-related measures, and frataxin expression, for earlier treatment evaluation.
papers.why: The review identifies tested NRF2-modulating interventions and candidate biomarkers for monitoring therapeutic responses in Friedreich ataxia.

papers.title: Differential expression of PGC-1α and metabolic sensors suggest age-dependent induction of mitochondrial biogenesis in Friedreich ataxia fibroblasts.
papers.summary: In fibroblasts from three patients with Friedreich ataxia, the paper found oxidative stress, reduced ATP and antioxidant deficiencies, while mitochondrial-biogenesis signaling was increased in the two older patient cultures but absent in the youngest. Idebenone suppressed PGC-1α and mtTFA expression in the two responsive cultures, and the authors propose that age-dependent compensatory mitochondrial biogenesis may contribute to cardiac disease evolution.
papers.why: The study provides patient-derived FRDA cellular measurements of oxidative stress and mitochondrial biogenesis plus data showing that idebenone alters these responses.

papers.title: Frataxin-deficient neurons and mice models of Friedreich ataxia are improved by TAT-MTScs-FXN treatment.
papers.summary: In frataxin-depleted rat dorsal root ganglion neurons and two mouse models of Friedreich ataxia, the mitochondrial frataxin replacement therapy TAT-MTScs-FXN restored several mitochondrial and neuronal readouts, including HSP60 processing, succinate dehydrogenase activity, reduced apoptosis, neurite integrity, and cell survival. In conditional frataxin-knockout mice, intraperitoneal TAT-MTScs-FXN at 10 mg/kg significantly increased mean lifespan, while 4 mg/kg and intravenous treatment did not significantly improve survival.
papers.why: TAT-MTScs-FXN improved neuronal survival and mitochondrial pathology in patient-relevant cells and restored muscle mitochondrial activity while extending lifespan in Friedreich ataxia mice.

papers.title: Pharmacological screening using an FXN-EGFP cellular genomic reporter assay for the therapy of Friedreich ataxia.
papers.summary: The study established an FXN-EGFP genomic reporter screening assay and identified cisplatin, camptothecin, deferiprone, resveratrol, and several other compounds that increased FXN expression and frataxin levels in Friedreich ataxia cells. Resveratrol also increased human FXN mRNA and frataxin protein in the brain of the YG8R humanized mouse model, but the response occurred only at 200 mg/kg and no clinical benefit was tested in this paper.
papers.why: The study develops and validates a high-throughput FXN expression assay, screens compounds, and confirms increased frataxin in FRDA patient cells and a disease mouse model.

papers.title: Cellular, molecular and functional characterisation of YAC transgenic mouse models of Friedreich ataxia.
papers.summary: The paper characterises three human FXN yeast artificial chromosome transgenic mouse lines carrying normal or expanded intronic GAA repeats. YG8R and YG22R mice reproduce reduced frataxin expression, somatic GAA-repeat instability, progressive motor and gait deficits, and aspects of abnormal glucose handling, while copy-number variation, body weight, sex, and tissue-specific expression complicate interpretation; the models are proposed as resources for FRDA mechanism studies and preclinical therapeutic testing.
papers.why: The paper experimentally characterizes three transgenic Friedreich ataxia mouse models with neurological, metabolic, molecular, and repeat-instability phenotypes.

papers.title: The History of Deferiprone (L1) and the Paradigm of the Complete Treatment of Iron Overload in Thalassaemia.
papers.summary: This review identifies deferiprone as an orally administered iron chelator with tissue penetration that can remove excess iron, including focal mitochondrial iron deposits in Friedreich ataxia. It reports encouraging but nonspecific clinical prospects for Friedreich ataxia and emphasizes that weekly blood-cell monitoring is required because agranulocytosis is the drug’s most severe toxicity.
papers.why: The review documents extensive clinical use of deferiprone for iron overload and explicitly identifies it as a leading therapeutic selected for Friedreich ataxia.

papers.title: Multiple mechanisms underpin cerebral and cerebellar white matter deficits in Friedreich ataxia: The IMAGE-FRDA study.
papers.summary: The IMAGE-FRDA study demonstrates widespread microstructural and macrostructural white-matter abnormalities in individuals with Friedreich ataxia, most prominently in cerebellar and brainstem regions and along cerebello-thalamo-cerebral pathways. Diffusion, magnetization-transfer, and volumetric MRI indices showed partly independent relationships with disease severity, onset age, and GAA1 repeat length, supporting multiple underlying disease processes while requiring histological and longitudinal validation.
papers.why: The study validates multiple MRI measures in Friedreich ataxia and relates white-matter microstructural and volumetric abnormalities to severity and age of onset.

papers.title: Clinical management guidelines for Friedreich ataxia: best practice in rare diseases.
papers.summary: This paper reports the development of updated clinical management guidelines for Friedreich ataxia using a rare-disease adaptation of the GRADE framework. The guideline-development process combined direct and indirect published evidence, natural-history registry data, structured clinician observations, expert consensus, and input from people with Friedreich ataxia, producing 130 recommendations and 95 best-practice statements despite predominantly low-certainty evidence.
papers.why: The paper provides an evidence-graded care framework, recommendations, and reusable natural-history and patient-engagement methods for Friedreich ataxia.

papers.title: Human frataxin, the Friedreich ataxia deficient protein, interacts with mitochondrial respiratory chain.
papers.summary: The paper shows that frataxin physically interacts with mitochondrial respiratory complexes I, II and III, while reduced frataxin in Friedreich ataxia cells is associated particularly with loss of complex I-associated iron–sulfur and radical EPR signals. Expression of the frataxin-like Thermus thermophilus protein Nqo15 increased maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity in FRDA patient fibroblasts, providing proof-of-concept for targeting respiratory complex I.
papers.why: Expressing the Nqo15 protein ameliorated the mitochondrial respiratory phenotype in FRDA patient cells, while the study also supplies mechanistic assays and cellular models.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Leriglitazone in Patients With Friedreich Ataxia: A Phase 2 Double-Blind, Randomized Controlled Trial (FRAMES).
papers.summary: This 48-week phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study found that leriglitazone did not improve the primary MRI endpoint of cervical spinal cord area in patients with Friedreich ataxia. Secondary imaging and biochemical endpoints suggested possible effects on dentate nucleus iron accumulation and spinal cord metabolic status, but these findings were exploratory or nominal, while peripheral edema was frequent.
papers.why: A randomized placebo-controlled trial directly tested leriglitazone in genetically confirmed Friedreich ataxia and quantified clinical and MRI outcomes, though the primary endpoint was negative.

papers.title: Epigenetic-based therapies for Friedreich ataxia.
papers.summary: This review concludes that Friedreich ataxia is accompanied by epigenetic silencing of FXN, including increased DNA methylation, repressive histone modifications, and reduced activating marks. It describes several epigenetic strategies that raise FXN expression in FRDA cells or mouse models, while emphasizing incomplete mechanistic certainty, limited delivery, and potential off-target toxicities.
papers.why: The paper describes concrete epigenetic strategies developed to reverse pathogenic FXN silencing and restore frataxin expression in FRDA.

papers.title: Expression of human frataxin is regulated by transcription factors SRF and TFAP2.
papers.summary: The paper identifies SRF and TFAP2 as transcription factors that bind directly to regulatory sequences near the human FXN promoter and increase frataxin mRNA and protein expression in transfected cell models. Over-expression of either factor increased frataxin mRNA in Friedreich ataxia patient lymphoblasts, but effects were cell-type dependent, and the data do not demonstrate clinical treatment or disease modification.
papers.why: Direct experiments in Friedreich ataxia patient lymphoblasts and other cells showed that SRF and TFAP2 overexpression increases frataxin mRNA and protein, identifying gene-therapy or small-molecule activation targets.

papers.title: Efficacy of Epoetin Alfa in Patients With Friedreich's Ataxia
papers.summary:
Friedreich's ataxia is a rare genetic disorder characterized by severe neurological disability and cardiomyopathy. Friedreich's ataxia is the consequence of frataxin deficiency. Although several drugs have been proposed, there is no available treatment. It was recently demonstrated that erythropoietin can increase the intracellular levels of frataxin in an in-vitro model.

The present project is aimed at testing the possible therapeutic approach of erythropoietin, which is an already available and commercialized drug. The investigators will perform both in-vitro and in-vivo tests, in order to

papers.title: A First in Human Study of RT001 in Patients With Friedreich's Ataxia
papers.summary: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics of RT001 in patients with Friedreich's ataxia.

papers.title: Safety and Efficacy of EPI-743 in Patients With Friedreich's Ataxia
papers.summary: The purpose of this study is to examine the effects of EPI-743 on visual function and neurologic function in patients with Friedreich's ataxia.

papers.title: An Open-Label Study of CTI-1601 in Subjects With Friedreich's Ataxia
papers.summary: An open label study designed to evaluate the safety, PK, PD, and clinical effects of long-term daily administration of CTI-1601 enrolling adolescent and adult patients with FRDA who have participated in a prior clinical study of CTI-1601 as well as children (age 2 years and older), adolescents and adults with FRDA who have not participated in a prior clinical study of CTI-1601.

papers.title: Efficacy of Riluzole in Hereditary Cerebellar Ataxia
papers.summary:
The hereditary cerebellar ataxias include diverse neurodegenerative disorders. Hereditary ataxias can be divided into autosomal dominant ataxias (ADCAs), autosomal recessive ataxias (ARCAs), X-linked, and mitochondrial ataxias on the basis of mode of inheritance. The key feature in all these disorders is ataxia typically characterised by poor balance, hand incoordination, postural or kinetic tremor, dysarthria and dysphagia.

To date no treatment has been shown to slow progression of the disease and symptomatic therapies are limited to few options that are partially effective.

papers.title: A Study of Vatiquinone for the Treatment of Participants With Friedreich Ataxia
papers.summary: The primary objective of the study is to assess the pharmacokinetics (PK) and safety of vatiquinone administered in participants with Friedreich ataxia (FA) younger than 7 years.

papers.title: A Study to Learn More About the Effects and Long-Term Safety of Omaveloxolone (BIIB141) in Children and Teens With Friedreich's Ataxia
papers.summary:
In this study, researchers will learn more about omaveloxolone, also known as BIIB141 or SKYCLARYS®. Omaveloxolone is already approved for people with Friedreich's Ataxia (FA) who are 16 years of age or older. However, it is not yet available for younger teens and children. The main goal of this study is to learn how omaveloxolone affects symptoms of FA and its safety in younger participants between the ages of 2 and 15 years old.

The main questions researchers want to answer in this study are:

* How does omaveloxolone affect the participants' FA symptoms?
* How does the body process omavelo

papers.title: EPI-743 in Friedreich's Ataxia Point Mutations
papers.summary: The purpose of this study is to evaluate the effects of EPI-743 in patients with Friedreich's Ataxia point mutations

papers.title: Safety Study of Idebenone to Treat Friedreich's Ataxia
papers.summary:
This study will determine the highest dose of idebonone that can safely be given to patients with Friedrich's ataxia, an inherited degenerative disease that causes loss of muscle coordination, speech problems, weakness and sensory loss. Enlargement of the left ventricle (the large pumping chamber of the heart) is also common in this disease. In studies in France and Canada, patients with Friedrich's ataxia who were given idebonone, an antioxidant similar to the dietary supplement coenzyme Q, had a decrease in the size of their left ventricle.
